Chapter 9. The Postmodern Turn—Doubt, Deconstruction, and the Challenge of Relativism.
As we neared the end of the twentieth century, something shifted in the air. Those big, sweeping stories that once helped people make sense of the world—they started to crumble. Postmodernism brought a new vibe: a healthy dose of skepticism and a touch of irony became the mood of the age.
Imagine a college student, sitting in a crowded lecture hall, surrounded by a hundred different opinions. Suddenly, doubting everything becomes second nature. Truth? Well, that's just a matter of perspective. Morality? Maybe it's just a matter of personal taste. Instead of clear answers, there's endless debate. It can feel like nothing is certain anymore.
You could see this shift everywhere, especially in art and literature. Boundaries faded away. Playwrights blended comedy and tragedy, mixed history with fantasy, and left audiences wondering what was real and what was fiction. Even designers, working on ads for global brands, grabbed images from every culture and every era, creating a kind of visual patchwork. The world started to look like a giant collage of borrowed ideas and meanings.
For some folks, this newfound freedom was exciting. Suddenly, you could invent yourself—pick your own identity, choose your own path. But for others, it felt exhausting, even overwhelming. Without a common story to hold onto, life could seem fragmented, a bit aimless. Take a teacher, for example, trying her best to guide her students. When they ask those tough questions about what's right and wrong, she doesn't have the old certainties to lean on anymore.
The biblical worldview, which once sat at the core of Western culture, now became just one choice among many. Faith turned into something deeply personal, almost private—no longer a public foundation for life. People kept searching for meaning, but the answers seemed further and further out of reach.
Yet, even in this sea of doubt and endless questions, something deeper lingered. People still yearned for truth, for connection, for that sense of purpose that could actually stand up to real life. So, while the story of Western culture felt fractured and uncertain, it was far from over. The questions that have haunted the West for centuries—they're still here, still waiting for an answer.
